title: Values, names, and surprising mutation
outcome: Predict Ruby truthiness and explain when two names share one object.

exercises.title: Find and fix the bug
exercises.prompt: A settings reader uses config[:send_email] || true. A report groups items using Hash.new([]). Explain the two independent bugs and repair both.

exercises.title: Change one condition
exercises.prompt: You dup a hash containing an array, then append to the copied array. What happens to the original? How would you avoid shared nested state?

trace.title: Variable name
trace.detail: A Ruby variable holds a reference to an object. Assignment copies the reference, not the whole object. If two names point to one array, changing that array is visible through both names. Reassigning one name points it somewhere else.

trace.title: Follow the middle steps
trace.detail:
Draw two arrows to the same array before the append. After second is reassigned, draw its arrow to a new array. The first arrow did not move.

Hash.new([]) uses one shared default object and does not insert missing keys when you read them. The block form above creates and stores a separate array for each new key. dup copies only one level; nested arrays can still be shared.

trace.title: Check the result
trace.detail: A method ending in ! often warns about a surprising or dangerous variant; it is not a universal promise of mutation. Read the method contract. freeze is also shallow unless you freeze nested objects yourself.
